Context/Background: To find novel treatments and drug combinations that could effectively target colorectal cancer cells (CRCs) and lower the probability of disease relapse, we designed multiple different combinations between cisplatin, cannabidiol (CBD), and intermittent serum starvation (ISS) on colorectal cancer cell lines. We analyzed differentially expressed genes and affected pathways in colorectal cancer cell lines to understand further the potential molecular mechanisms behind the treatments and their interactions.
Prompt: Based on the results of the differential expression analysis of Cisplatin vs DMSO in colorectal cancer cells, run a pathway overrepresentation analysis for statistically significant genes (up and down combined) against the Reactome database. Then, provide a discussion of any relevant affected pathways, highlighting important up and down regulated genes in each.  Focus on any mechanisms by which Cisplatin may alter cancer related pathways.
output_text:
Introduction/Context  
We analyzed RNA‐seq data from colorectal cancer (CRC) cell lines treated with cisplatin versus DMSO (ijms-24-14743-v2_crc_cells_cisplatin_vs_dmso_DEG.csv). After DESeq2, 1 018 genes passed padj < 0.05. We ran an over-representation analysis (ORA) of these significant genes against the Reactome_Pathways_2024 library. Below are the top enriched pathways, their gene overlaps, adjusted p-values, and the constituent genes.  

Keywords  
• p53 signaling  
• Cell cycle arrest  
• Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress  
• Apoptosis  
• Extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling  

Candidate Genes  
TP53, CDKN1A, GADD45A, BAX, ATF4, DDIT3  

Top Reactome ORA Results (padj < 0.01)  
| Term                                                              | Overlap | Adj P-value     | Genes                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------|---------|-----------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| TP53 Regulates Transcription of Cell Cycle Genes                  | 19 / 49 | 1.15 × 10^–9    | PLK3; BTG2; CDKN1A; CDKN1B; CNOT6L; PCNA; PRMT1; GADD45A; PLK2; TFDP1; RGCC; CCNE2; PCBP4; EP300; BAX; SFN; CNOT8; ZNF385A; E2F7 |
| Transcriptional Regulation by TP53                                | 51 / 362| 1.67 × 10^–8    | GPI; BTG2; CDKN1A; CDKN1B; PRKAG2; PRDM1; TRIAP1; GLS; PIDD1; ING2; SESN1; EP300; ZNF385A; BNIP3L; CNOT6L; CSNK2A1; PRMT1; TSC1; DDB2; TFDP1; CCNE2; RRM2B; PCNA; UBB; PCBP4; TP53INP1; PMAIP1; SFN; MTA2; RFFL; E2F7; MBD3; PLK3; TIGAR; GADD45A; PLK2; TNFRSF10C; TNFRSF10B; TNFRSF10A; SSRP1; MTOR; HIPK2; RGCC; TP53I3; CCNG1; MDM2; FAS; TCEA1; BAX; CNOT8; ATR |
| TP53 Regulates Transcription of Genes Involved in G2 Cell Cycle Arrest | 8 / 18  | 3.34 × 10^–4    | PCNA; TFDP1; GADD45A; PRMT1; BAX; EP300; SFN; ZNF385A                                                               |
| ATF4 Activates Genes in Response to Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress  | 9 / 28  | 1.09 × 10^–3    | EXOSC5; EXOSC4; DDIT3; ASNS; ATF6; ATF3; DCP2; HERPUD1; ATF4                                                       |
| Response of EIF2AK1 (HRI) to Heme Deficiency                      | 6 / 15  | 3.91 × 10^–3    | EIF2AK1; DDIT3; ASNS; ATF5; ATF3; ATF4                                                                           |
| Gluconeogenesis                                                   | 8 / 26  | 2.45 × 10^–3    | GPI; TPI1; PGK1; ALDOC; ENO1; ENO2; ALDOA; GAPDH                                                                 |

Discussion  
1. p53-Driven Cell Cycle and Apoptosis: The strongest ORA signals involve p53-mediated transcription (e.g., “TP53 Regulates Transcription of Cell Cycle Genes”, padj = 1.15 × 10^–9). Key effector genes—CDKN1A (↑ log2FC 1.21), GADD45A (↑ 0.41), BAX (↑ 0.74)—are upregulated, consistent with cisplatin-induced DNA damage leading to p53-dependent G1/S and G2/M arrest and apoptosis.  
2. ER Stress/Integrated Stress Response: “ATF4 Activates Genes in Response to ER Stress” and the HRI pathway are enriched (padj = 1.09 × 10^–3 and 3.91 × 10^–3). Although ATF4 itself is modestly downregulated (log2FC –0.15), its downstream target DDIT3 (CHOP) is significantly altered, suggesting that cisplatin perturbs protein-folding homeostasis and induces an unfolded protein response.  
3. Metabolic Rewiring: Enrichment of “Gluconeogenesis” (padj = 2.45 × 10^–3) implies shifts in central carbon metabolism, possibly reflecting a stress-adaptation phenotype. upregulated glycolytic/gluconeogenic enzymes (GPI, PGK1, GAPDH) may support survival under cisplatin stress.  
4. Extracellular Matrix and Cell-Surface Interactions: Strong GSEA-based up-enriched pathways (NES > 2.6) include “Cell Surface Interactions at the Vascular Wall” and “ECM Proteoglycans,” indicating remodeling of adhesion and microenvironment interfaces. These changes could influence drug uptake, dissemination, or immune cell engagement.  
5. Innate Immune Signaling Down-Modulation: GSEA shows downregulation of TLR4-mediated cascades (TRIF- and MyD88-dependent, NES ≈ –1.98), suggesting cisplatin may suppress TLR4-driven inflammatory signaling, with potential implications for immunogenic cell death.  

Overall, cisplatin triggers a p53-centric response—upregulating cell cycle inhibitors and pro-apoptotic factors—while also engaging ER stress and metabolic adaptation programs. Concurrent remodeling of ECM and dampening of TLR4 innate signaling may modulate the tumor microenvironment and immune interactions, offering mechanistic entry points for combination therapies (e.g., ER stress modulators, immune adjuvants, or ECM-targeted agents).
